4965.dq: Stress is on the first full vowel syllable of the root. [...] These rules work within the root. [...] The "vowel harmony" rule does not apply over morpheme or word boundaries. (p. 111; the data are 'About 230 two-syllable and three-syllable words in frame', p. 110; intonation is treated separately in 4.3.3)
4965.dloc: Section 4.3.1 'Stress', pp. 109-112: opening p. 109 (last paragraph) and p. 110; 'vowel harmony' rule p. 110 (last two paragraphs); stress rule and examples p. 111 (first paragraph, example lists, editor's fn 3); secondary stress p. 111 (last paragraph); reduplication p. 112 (first paragraph) (image PDF)
4965.heavy: Not a syllable-weight criterion. The stress rule as printed is 'Stress is on the first full vowel syllable of the root' (p. 111), but the full/reduced status of a vowel is not a lexical property: the central vowel is 'not... an independent phoneme' (p. 109), 'neither are phonemic' (p. 111), and it is produced by the 'vowel harmony' rule (p. 110) from the relative openness or identity of the two successive vowels. The conditioning of stress is therefore the vowels' relative height/identity: V1 more open than V2 -> V1 stays full and is stressed (['karek], ['atok], ['komuŋ]); V1 more closed than V2, or the two identical -> V1 reduces to [ə] and stress is on the second syllable ([tən'tar], [nə'nol], [kə'lu], [nəm'ba]). The printed wording of the harmony rule and of editor's fn 3 has the open/closed polarity inverted relative to these examples. Residue the source does not derive: /ta.'pon/ [təpo:n] 'to squeeze' (p. 110; a > o yet reduced), 'u could sometimes occur in this less prominent postion' unreduced (p. 110), and word-initial [ə] whose underlying vowel 'is not obvious' (/arpm.a/ [ərpm'a] 'to be', /ə.nu/ [ə'nu] 'female', p. 111). Stress correlates: at least two of louder, longer, less ballistic (slower amplitude decay), non-centralized vowel.
4965.dflt: not applicable (segmental conditioning, not weight). Every root has a stressable full-vowel syllable, since the central vowel 'never occurs in one-syllable words or in word final syllables' (p. 109).
4965.prule: Within the root, stress falls on the first syllable whose vowel is a full (non-central) vowel, and which syllable that is depends on the vowels of the successive syllables, not on syllable weight: as the paper's own example lists show it, when V1 is more open than V2 the first vowel stays full and takes the stress (['karek] 'hen, rooster', ['atok] 'white ant', ['komuŋ] 'a bird', ['wendiŋ] 'junction'); when V1 is more closed than V2 or the two vowels are phonemically identical, V1 is reduced to the non-phonemic central vowel [ə] and stress falls on the second syllable ([tən'tar] 'miserable', [nə'nol] 'mushroom', [kə'lu] 'bottom', [nəm'ba] 'dog', [tə'kor] 'not red'). Stress is cued by at least two of louder, longer, less ballistic (slower amplitude decay), non-central vowel; stress and the central vowel are both non-phonemic. The printed 'vowel harmony' rule (p. 110) and the editor's fn 3 (p. 111) state the open/closed polarity the other way round from the examples; the later Hemmilä & Luoma grammar, as carried by Wood 2012:7, states it the examples' way (V1 more open than V2 -> initial, otherwise final).
4965.srule: In a three-syllable word stressed on its first syllable, the third syllable usually carries a secondary stress (/wa.rim-pen/ [ˈwarimˌpen] 'young person'); in reduplicated words all parts are stressed, the first with primary stress (/naŋ-naŋ/ [ˈnaŋˌnaŋ] 'sing-sing'). The source says nothing about longer words or about trisyllables stressed on the second syllable.

4967.dq: Como é redundante, podemos considerar que a acentuação tanto de intensidade como de altura contribui como um reforço perceptual do peso silábico na tarefa da demarcação das palavras fonológicas em todos os registros, e dos lexemas nos registros fonoestilísticos maxiarticulados. [p.70] a nível lexical, a sílaba leve é sempre não-acentuada e a sílaba pesada é sempre acentuada.
4967.heavy: a sílaba pesada é sempre do tipo [CVC], [CVː] ou [CVV̯]; a sílaba leve é sempre do tipo [CV̆] (p.22) — heavy = closed syllable, long vowel, or diphthong; light = open short-vowel syllable.
4967.dflt: not applicable: the template forbids lexemes without a heavy syllable (*[CV̆ CV̆]); every lexeme has exactly one heavy syllable.
4967.prule: Stress (strong intensity + high pitch) falls on the heavy syllable (CVC, CVː or CVV) of the lexeme; a light CV syllable is unstressed with low pitch. Since every Chapakura lexeme is #(CV)H#, the one heavy syllable is always lexeme-final: monosyllables are stressed, disyllables have final stress. Stated family-wide by Lima 1997 and applied to Urupá through her reading of Nimuendajú's accent-marked spellings.
4967.srule: None: one stress per lexeme (= phonological word). 'uma sílaba leve é átona e possui um tom baixo... uma sílaba pesada é tônica e possui um tom alto. /#(σ)σ#/ → [(σ̀)ˈσ́]' — every lexeme is at most disyllabic (light + stressed heavy); the grave/acute in the formula are low/high pitch marks, not degrees of stress; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described. Longer items in Nimuendajú's 1925 Urupá list are lexeme strings, each lexeme with its own stressed heavy syllable, unranked by the source.
4967.quote: Nas línguas Chapakura, a acentuação dos lexemas é dedutível do peso silábico - o único fator prosódico fonológico nessa família lingüística. Portanto, o acento não é fonológico por ser previsível. [...] A atualização fonética da acentuação lexical obedece às seguintes regras: (a) uma sílaba leve é átona e possui um tom baixo. Em outras palavras, carrega um acento de intensidade (“stress”) fraco e um acento de altura (“pitch”) baixo; (b) uma sílaba pesada é tônica e possui um tom alto. Em outras palavras, carrega um acento de intensidade (“stress”) forte e um acento de altura (“pitch”) alto. /…
4967.idn: Urupá (abbrev. URU), an extinct Chapakura language of the upper Jamari / Urupá headwaters (Rondônia, Brazil); §3.9 'Fonemas e sons do Urupá'; the accent rule itself is stated for 'as línguas Chapakura' as a whole (Panchapakura); data: No first-hand Urupá data: Lima analysed the six dead languages from old spellings…
4967.exq_: a nível lexical, a sílaba leve é sempre não-acentuada e a sílaba pesada é sempre acentuada. (p.70) — the only qualification is a register process, not a lexical exception: nos registros médio e hipoarticulados, pode haver encurtamento vocálico e fusão de lexemas monossílabos (p.23).
4967.tone: Not a tone language: syllable weight is 'o único fator prosódico fonológico'; high pitch is a correlate of stress on the heavy syllable and low pitch of the unstressed light syllable (p.24). ILLA 2000 measured intensity/pitch instrumentally only in five living languages, not Urupá.

4968.dloc: Chapter 2 Phonology, §2.13.2 'Stress', pp. 117-123; supporting statements p. 3 Introduction, §2.14 p. 123, and the areal-features paragraph of the contact section (p. 10).
4968.prule: Main word stress falls on the penultimate syllable in morphologically simple words (quantity-insensitive, counted from the right edge); Hannß repeats this as the language's tendency (p. 3) and lists penultimate stress among the areal features shared with Aymara and Quechua. Under affixation the archival data show only tendencies: a monosyllabic stem + bisyllabic suffix takes double stress or shifts stress to the new penult; a monosyllabic stem + monosyllabic suffix keeps stress in situ (then often not on the penult); bisyllabic stems either keep or shift stress with no clear pattern; verbal stress is 'almost impossible' to regularise, usually stays on the stem, sometimes shifts to the final syllable (monosyllabic verb + monosyllabic suffix, e.g. imperative onái); final stress is otherwise exceptional and emphatic; declarative -cay is always unstressed.
4968.srule: Hannß does not distinguish primary from secondary stress; she reports words with double or triple ('multiple') stress in the archival transcriptions, as tendencies with counterexamples: most trisyllabic nominal stems are doubly stressed, mainly on the first and third syllables (fn. 269: sometimes first and second), unchanged under suffixation; a monosyllabic nominal stem + bisyllabic suffix may be stressed on both stem and suffix-initial syllable (hux'-kama 'while going', am-tani 'with you'), else stress shifts to the new penult; a single-stressed trisyllabic stem + bisyllabic suffix may carry up to three stresses ((221) pi.kil.ta.ni-sta.ni-ki); bisyllabic nominal stems never take double stress; verbs optionally add a second stress on 1sg -u/-a or in-group -acu; purposive -srap'a always bears stress on its own first syllable.

4978.dq: Marichelle 1902: 6: 'parce-que la particule lu prenant l'accent tonique, peut-être considérée comme faisant partie du mot' (the accent is placed within the dictionary word, prefix + stem). By contrast the modern lengthening statement is phrasal: 'A single vowel is perceived long when it is in a penultimate syllable position of a phrase or sentence-final word' (Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008: 164).
4978.prule: No word-stress rule in the modern description: Civili is treated as a tone language (H/L tones, unmarked in the orthography) whose only positional prominence is vowel lengthening on the penultimate syllable of a phrase- or sentence-final word (Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008 Rule 5). The one stress statement is Marichelle 1902's 'accent tonique de pénultième', a word-level penultimate accent presupposed as a spelling rationale (prefix written together with a monosyllabic stem when it carries the accent: lu-to 'spoon', bi-gni 'faces', bi-ka 'beds').

4978.tone: Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008 (Stellenbosch PhD, Civili of Mayumba/Gabon) uses H/L tone throughout (abbreviations p. xxi; 'the marking of tones and other suprasegmental features at the orthographic level does not occur'), cites Blanchon 1990 for the tone inventory (Ndinga-Koumba-Binza & Roux 2009: 'consonants, vowels and tones': 'tones are not marked in Civili orthography'), and states no word-stress rule for Civili: stress appears only as a cross-linguistic factor in vowel duration (p. 133, Gussenhoven 2001 quote; p. 145 list of factors 'j. stress', p. 146 'd. tones') and in the phrase 'an unstressed nominal prefix syllable' (p. 30, citing Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2000) as a context for [a]-reduction. Penultimate prominence is described as phrase-level lengthening (p. 159: 'in a phrase- or sentence penultimate syllable the duration of the vowel is longer than in other positions'; p. 164 Rule 5, V -> [long] / __CV##; p. 146: long vowels 'only in the first syllable of disyllabic words or penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words'). Marichelle 1902 never mentions tone ('ton' occurs only as the French possessive; 'intonation' once s.v. Kunu-kuna); his 'accent tonique de pénultième' (31 'accent' hits, dozens of entries 'prend l'accent de (la) pénult.') is a dictionary convention for prefix + monosyllabic stem. The same author's grammar (Marichelle 1907, 'Accent tonique' pp. 10-11) states the rule explicitly, and it is initial in the word without its particle (which coincides with the penult only for disyllables such as 'Li mémé ... prononcez : mémé') rather than penultimate once the word has three or more syllables: 'La langue vilie a l'accent tonique. Les radicaux monosyllabes, à part de rares exceptions, laissent cet accent à leur particule ... Ex. ḳika, le lit. Ḳi est long, parce qu'il prend l'accent' (p. 10); 'Les mots de deux syllabes, ont l'accent sur la pénultième ... Les mots de trois syllabes, ont l'accent sur l'antépénultième, en général. Futika, plier, fu est long. Les mots de quatre syllabes ont, en général, l'accent sur la première syllabe, et parfois sur la troisième ... Quand un mot, un verbe spécialement, prend un suffixe, l'accent se reporte sur la première voyelle du radical. Sāla, sālila, sālilila. Est excepté le suffixe anga, qui prend l'accent ; sálilānga' (p. 11). Marichelle equates the accented syllable with length ('est long') and the 1907 chapter never mentions tone, so his 'accent' is the missionary perception of vowel length on the first syllable of the stem (on the prefix when the stem is monosyllabic), with the placement for monosyllabic stems reading as lexical tone; it is not a phrase-penultimate lengthening rule of the Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008 kind (p. 164 Rule 5), and its antepenultimate 'fu' in futika does not match Ndinga-Koumba-Binza's distribution of long vowels (p. 146: first syllable of disyllabic words or penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words).

tn.translation: If that is so, Ci-Vili nominals would have, for all themes of more than one syllable, only two types: Type I: H-H(L)n, Type II: H-L(L)n. Since the prefix is always high and the syllables after the theme-initial one always low, the only relevant classification criterion is the high or low tone of the radical syllable. In fact, if one keeps to citation forms, as Ndamba seems to do, all nominals divide neatly between these two types.

tn.quote: en VinC, il y a très peu de différence d’intensité entre les syllabes au niveau lexical. … dans des paires polysyllabiques, ni la durée ni l’intensité ne semblent avoir d‘effet sur l’interprétation sémantique. Par conséquent, les mouvements d’accent mélodique ne signalent pas seulement la proéminence des syllabes, ils transmettent également des sens non ambigus. … les deux mots portent l’accent tonique sur la première syllabe … Le signe diacritique ˋ indique que l’accent mélodique est descendant, ˆ indique un accent mélodique montant descendant.
tn.translation: in VinC there is very little difference in intensity between syllables at the lexical level. … in polysyllabic pairs, neither duration nor intensity seems to have any effect on the semantic interpretation. Consequently, the pitch-accent movements do not only signal the prominence of syllables, they also convey unambiguous meanings. … both words carry the stress on the first syllable … The diacritic ˋ indicates that the pitch accent is falling, ˆ indicates a rising-falling pitch accent.

4982.tone: Hofmeister acknowledges 'musikalischer Ton' but calls it less essential than in other Sudanic and some Bantu languages and marks it only for 'especially important' words in his word list (section IV, p. 5). The modern SIL orthography statement (Thwing 1981/2004, p. 4) gives a three-level tone system (high, mid, low, plus contours; tone marked on both halves of long vowels; downstep unmarked) and says nothing about stress or accent. The 1918 accent statement is an early pre-phonemic description of a language now described as tonal; no modern source confirms or denies word stress, so no source conflict is recorded and the classification is not overridden to tone or pitch accent; confidence low.

tn.quote: Vute has three tone levels, H, M, L, plus downstep. Vute has both lexical and grammatical tone. In the Vute (Vɨ́tè) orthography, H tone is written with an acute accent over the vowel/syllable nucleus, L tone is indicated with a grave accent over the vowel, the falling tones (HL or HM) are marked with a circumflex accent, M tone is unmarked as are the rising tones unless they occur on long vowels, when each vowel is marked with the corresponding tone. Downstep is also unmarked. In addition, Vute has some three tone units on single syllables containing two or more morphemes ...

4983.tone: Leenhardt's only prosodic remark on Wamoang is the lexical pitch pair le 'nous' (bas) vs le 'eux' (haut) under the template heading 'Accent et ton'; he does not call the language tonal, gives no other pitch-marked form, and says nothing about accent/stress. His general chapter (p. 11, line 48, verified by C) defers accent and tone to each language chapter: 'Il reste à connaître l'accent, le ton, et les particularités phonétiques de chaque langue. On en trouvera le détail au chapitre réservé à chacune de celles-ci.' The parallel §2 in the Pwapwa chapter is equally one pair ('neole = le nôtre: bas et sourd' / 'neole = le leur: haut et sonore'), so the heading is a fixed template whose content is whatever pitch pair he noted. Voegelin & Voegelin 1964: 63 (verified by C) restate the pair second-hand as 'Thirteen vowel symbols are used; vowels occur with at least two phonemic distinctions of tone.' Rivierre 1972 (BSLP 67: 302, verified by C) calls the cluster Waamwang belonged to 'les dialectes sans tons de Voh-Koné'. One pronoun pair from a 3-speaker questionnaire, unconfirmed by any later worker and contradicted by the specialist's classification of the sister dialects, does not establish a tone system; hence not determinable from the sources rather than tone or pitch accent.

4984.dq: Peter (1990: 115-117, 120-121) justifie cette analyse en expliquant que seulement quatre schèmes tonals – H, B, HB, BH – sont attestés sur les noms dissyllabiques simples, et qu’il n’existe pas de paires minimales tonales nominales opposant H contre ↑H (1). [tone is described on lexical words; no stress domain is described]
4984.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Waama is a two-tone language: contrastive H and B (low), with distinctive upstep (↑H) and downstep (↓B) partly due to floating low tones; the tone-bearing unit is the syllable (Peter 1990 analysed it as the moneme); lexical tone schemes on di-/trisyllabic nouns and verbs (HB, ↑HH, HH, BB, BH... on disyllabic nouns) are contrastive.

4984.tone: The whole report is about tone: two distinctive tones H and B (confirming Peter 1990 against the three-tone systems of the other Eastern Oti-Volta languages), distinctive upstep ↑H and downstep ↓B, floating B tones, TBU = syllable (§2.2, §3.2; Peter 1990's abstract says the moneme), tone schemes of disyllabic and trisyllabic nouns and verbs (§3.3-3.4), grammatical tone on pronouns and aspect markers. The word 'accent' occurs only for the orthographic grave/acute accent that writes tone on pronouns and particles; nothing anywhere on stress, intensity, prominence or an accented syllable, and no explicit denial of stress either. Cross-checks agree: Rowe 1991 p. 298 fn. 'There are two phonemic tones, high and low, but they are not written in the orthography'; Hartell 1993 alphabet page (image only) 'very high, high, low' tones; Eddyshaw 2024 §2.8.3 'Waama tonal data are scanty, and the sources differ'.

4990.sec_quote: In polysyllabic words with no long vowels, primary stress falls on the first syllable, and secondary stress falls on odd numbered syllables (e.g. yánjaràn 'old woman'). ... 4990.cfw: One first-hand description, checked against the source; of 5 other works consulted, Holmer's 1983 survey of the Wakka group (Part I §2.9, p. 5; the group includes Wakka-Wakka, of which Duungidjawu is a dialect) says stress is not significant in any of the languages surveyed, with a tendency to stress the second syllable in words or utterances of some length (Wakka-Wakka wangá ŋin janánde), Watson's 1944 pronunciation notes for his Kabi, Yugarabul, Wakka and Yugumbir vocabularies (p. 7) put accent generally on the first syllable and to a lesser degree on the third and mark accent on each Wakka headword, and the other 3 do not discuss stress.
